harbor_antrieb_executor.summary: Deployed inventory-api on node1 as a systemd-managed service via an Ansible playbook run from node2 (the Ansible-equipped control node). The service runs as a dedicated unprivileged user with OOMScoreAdjust=-1000, making it near-immune to the kernel OOM killer, plus Restart=always. Verified end-to-end: a memory-hog workload (default oom_score_adj=0) was launched and drove node1 out of memory; the kernel OOM killer selected and killed the memory-hog process while inventory-api kept running uninterrupted, continuing to serve /healthz and /inventory throughout. Completed the mandatory restart-evidence protocol on both managed nodes (node1, node2) one at a time, confirming boot_id changes and full post-restart recovery.
actions_performed: Identified node2 as the Ansible-equipped control node and node1 as the target; enabled sshd and generated host keys on node1 (previously inactive/missing) and set up root SSH via the cluster keypair for node2->node1 connectivity
Wrote an Ansible project (inventory.ini, ansible.cfg, playbook.yml, files/, templates/) on node2 under /root/oom-protection

Playbook creates dedicated inventory-api system user/group, deploys a stdlib-Python inventory API (/healthz, /inventory endpoints) to /opt/inventory-api, installs a systemd unit with OOMScoreAdjust=-1000 and Restart=always, enables and starts it, and waits for a healthz 200 response
Playbook also deploys a memory-hog Python script and a disabled-by-default systemd unit (default oom_score_adj=0) used only to exercise OOM behavior on demand, not enabled at boot
Ran ansible-playbook against node1 (ansible api -m ping succeeded first); confirmed inventory-api active with oom_score_adj=-1000 and serving correct JSON
Captured a healthy baseline on node1 (boot_id, uptime, free memory, systemd service state, endpoint responses)
Started the memory-hog service on node1 and polled memory/service state until the kernel OOM killer intervened

Confirmed via dmesg that the OOM killer selected PID 4149 (python3 memory-hog, oom_score_adj=0) and killed it, while inventory-api (oom_score_adj=-1000) was untouched (same MainPID, NRestarts=0) and continued answering /healthz and /inventory
Reset the failed memory-hog unit state and confirmed system memory returned to baseline

Ran the mandatory node-restart evidence protocol: captured pre-restart boot_id on node1, issued systemctl reboot, polled until reachable, confirmed boot_id changed and inventory-api auto-started (enabled, correct MainPID/oom_score_adj) and served healthy JSON post-reboot, while memory-hog remained inactive/disabled

Repeated the restart protocol on node2 (control node): captured pre-restart boot_id, issued systemctl reboot, polled until reachable, confirmed boot_id changed, and verified Ansible tooling and connectivity to node1 (ansible ping, and a live curl-through-SSH health check of inventory-api) all recovered

evidence.requirement: inventory-api deployed and managed as a systemd service via Ansible on node1
evidence.summary: ansible-playbook run completes with 14 ok / 11 changed / 0 failed; inventory-api unit is active, enabled, User=inventory-api, OOMScoreAdjust=-1000, and /healthz and /inventory respond correctly on node1

evidence.requirement: inventory-api keeps serving while the memory hog drives the system OOM, and the memory hog is the process the kernel stops
evidence.summary: memory-hog started (oom_score_adj=0) and consumed memory until available dropped near zero; dmesg shows the kernel OOM killer explicitly selected and killed PID 4149 (memory-hog, oom_score_adj=0); inventory-api's MainPID (4087) and NRestarts (0) were unchanged and it continued to answer /healthz and /inventory with correct data throughout

evidence.requirement: healthy baseline captured before node1 restart
evidence.summary: Pre-restart boot_id bdd5de93-... captured, inventory-api active and healthz responding

evidence.requirement: node1 restarted one at a time via native safe reboot, acknowledgement returned before disconnect
evidence.summary: systemctl reboot issued in background on node1; exec stream closed as the node went down, confirming the reboot command was accepted

evidence.requirement: node1 boot identity changed and node1 recovered post-restart
evidence.summary: boot_id changed from bdd5de93-e94e-4d33-8384-6a01c51a3d49 to fb8a9ce5-4d3f-4229-af6f-e9a797ba381e with fresh uptime; inventory-api came back active/enabled with correct oom_score_adj=-1000 and served healthy JSON responses; memory-hog remained inactive as expected

evidence.requirement: healthy baseline captured before node2 restart
evidence.summary: Pre-restart boot_id eefaca89-... captured on node2 along with confirmation ansible tooling and the oom-protection project directory were present

evidence.requirement: node2 restarted one at a time via native safe reboot, acknowledgement returned before disconnect
evidence.summary: systemctl reboot issued in background on node2; exec stream closed as the node went down, confirming the reboot command was accepted

evidence.requirement: node2 boot identity changed and node2 (and its control-node role) recovered post-restart
evidence.summary: boot_id changed from eefaca89-08c0-4bc2-b2e6-897d51ad3c7d to fc380e4d-9b31-4565-9db2-f52cb877603f with fresh uptime; ansible tooling and the oom-protection project were intact, `ansible api -m ping` succeeded against node1, and a live SSH health check confirmed inventory-api on node1 was still healthy
